review_method: Root complete source-read comparison of lattice proof and other completed modules, with accepted exact hypotheses/proof evidence. Each row records both actual conclusions/mechanisms and the specific distinction between filtered exponent counting and algebraic/analytic operations. Completed-only; no final whole293 claim.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Lattice counts exponent tuples below a reciprocal-weight threshold by fiber induction and scalar reciprocal estimates. Hasse derivatives use such tuples as operator orders but compute polynomial coefficients with natural binomial factors. Counting possible constraints does not establish any derivative vanishing or value; operator formulas do not yield the concentration count.
blocks.default_action: Keep finite-order counting separate from derivative algebra; share only actual exponent transport primitives.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Lattice counts all low-weight exponent tuples in a degree box independently of a polynomial. Taylor expands a fixed translated polynomial and computes its actual coefficients. A finite Taylor expansion can use the same box but does not bound how many orders lie under a weight cutoff without the separate lattice argument.
blocks.default_action: Retain exact polynomial expansion and quantitative counting as distinct interfaces.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Lattice estimates count selected exponent vectors, with a small-parameter trivial branch and large-parameter harmonic-sum induction. Coefficient norms sum absolute coefficient magnitudes, and evaluation bounds sum monomial magnitudes. Shared finite-sum/cardinality primitives do not identify unweighted concentration with coefficient-weighted or geometric majorants.
blocks.default_action: Share finite-set and finite-sum infrastructure but keep the actual summands, parameter regimes and inequalities separate.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Lattice uses reciprocal sums, square-root thresholds and exponent-box fibers. Wronskians use differential matrices, Vandermonde products and cancellation of leading polynomial degrees. Natural-number bookkeeping appears in both but does not identify their domains, hypotheses or proof steps.
blocks.default_action: No common full statement is indicated; retain existing generic finite-sum/product helpers without merging count estimates and determinant criteria.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: A low-weight lattice estimate bounds the number of admissible multi-indices. Generalized Wronskian existence selects particular derivatives with bounded total order after substitution and span arguments. Existence of a good selection cannot be inferred solely from an upper count of all allowable orders, and its independence argument does not count a reciprocal-weight box.
blocks.default_action: Preserve order-count budgets and nonvanishing selection as separate construction stages.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Last-coordinate fiber decomposition is a finite combinatorial bijection of exponent tuples. Distinguished-variable coefficient extraction decomposes polynomials and uses vector-space bases, then rational/integral factor descent. Their prefix/last-coordinate organization is analogous but the polynomial coefficient, independence and arithmetic information is absent from the counting bijection.
blocks.default_action: Share generic coordinate restriction/extension machinery where the exact maps agree; retain the different counting and coefficient-space conclusions.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Both modules use induction on the number of variables, but lattice induction sums counts of last-coordinate fibers and controls reciprocal shifts. Theta induction decomposes polynomials, estimates determinant indices, and balances one-variable/prefix extremal bounds through a nonlinear square-root recurrence. General induction packaging does not unify those mathematical recurrences.
blocks.default_action: Keep the separate recurrences; reuse only independently applicable finite-coordinate and scalar inequality APIs.

blocks.mechanism_comparison: Lattice controls the number of low-weight Hasse constraints selected later. The completed MainLemma opening constructs numerical error/cutoff budgets, estimates remainder coefficient growth, and counts polynomial coefficient choices. The number of constraints and number of polynomial choices are different finite sets; the strict pigeonhole budget compares them rather than equating them.
blocks.default_action: Retain concentration of derivative orders separately from polynomial-family size and analytic coefficient budgets.

special_pairs.comparison: The lattice theorem bounds the size of a low-weight subset of monomial indices by a fraction of the full degree box. The boxFamily theorem counts all independent coefficient assignments on that box as(B+1) to its size. These produce opposite sides of a later pigeonhole inequality, not the same count.
special_pairs.action: Preserve the generic lattice estimate and independent exact coefficient-family count; assemble their budgets only in the application.

special_pairs.comparison: The harmonic-grid sum estimate fixes a lattice lambda regime and improves a reciprocal denominator using sqrt_one_sub_inv_lt. Small-delta existence uses continuity near0 of a different dimension/error expression and selects a neighborhood. Both involve square roots but not a common limiting or summation argument.
special_pairs.action: Keep the finite-grid estimate separate from analytic parameter existence.

special_pairs.comparison: One partitions a filtered finite set into last-coordinate fibers and adds cardinalities. The other expands a polynomial into distinguished-variable powers with polynomial coefficients. A common coordinate split can support both, but counting fibers discards coefficient values and cannot reconstruct the polynomial.
special_pairs.action: Share coordinate equivalences when appropriate; retain separate finite-cardinality and polynomial-expansion APIs.

special_pairs.comparison: The lattice successor step applies the lower-dimensional count bound in every fiber and sums reciprocal losses. The Theta option theorem bounds an extremal index by a finite maximum of determinant-based bounds indexed by an auxiliary size. Sum of fiber counts and maximum of polynomial estimates are different aggregation mechanisms.
special_pairs.action: Do not merge the two dimension-recursion statements; retain the corresponding generic sum and finite-max infrastructure.

special_pairs.comparison: The first proves no exponent can meet a strictly negative low-weight cutoff. The second constructs an admissible index value from polynomial1 and coprime numerators when B>=1. The families and emptiness parameters differ; polynomial index nonnegativity is only an indirect shared lower-bound idea.
special_pairs.action: Keep exact family domains and cutoff/admissibility assumptions explicit.

special_pairs.comparison: The reciprocal-grid sum is bounded by pairing reflected indices and clearing positive denominators. The geometric sum is bounded through binomial expansion and lower bounds on natural binomial coefficients. Both sum nonnegative terms but use different symmetry and coefficient mechanisms.
special_pairs.action: Retain both scalar estimates; generic finite-sum monotonicity is the shared infrastructure, not the full result.
